paper.title_en: Optimizing Prompt Radio Counterpart Searches for Gravitational-Wave Events with the Deep Synoptic Array
paper.abstract_en: Prompt millisecond-duration coherent radio emission is proposed as a counterpart to neutron-star-containing compact mergers, produced before, during, or shortly after coalescence. Its detection would probe the plasma environment, magnetic fields, remnant evolution, and emission physics of these mergers. At GHz frequencies, dispersive delays can range from fractions of a second to several seconds, requiring the telescope to be on source before or soon after coalescence. Negative- or low-latency alerts, rapid response, and optimized pointing under uncertain, evolving localizations are therefore essential. We present a framework for prompt gravitational-wave follow-up with the upcoming Deep Synoptic Array (DSA), a sensitive, fast-slewing, wide-field GHz radio array. We simulate low-latency localization sequences and embed them in a follow-up environment with elevation, field-of-view, and slew constraints. We compare a reinforcement-learning pointing policy with a baseline that slews toward the highest-probability accessible region at each step. This peak-tracking rule is a strong, interpretable baseline for initial deployment, while the learned policy provides a complementary strategy for a subset of broad, multimodal, or arc-shaped localizations. At a random merger time, 37% of events are observable above $20^\circ$ elevation; among these, $\sim90\%$ of BNS events are successfully reached and tracked using zero-noise localization maps, decreasing to $\sim75\%$ with Gaussian-noise maps. We validate the optimized pointing trajectories on prototype DSA antennas. DSA follow-up can reach a fluence sensitivity of $\sim20$ mJy ms over a representative 700-1025 MHz sub-band, probing millisecond bursts with luminosities of approximately $10^{38}$ to $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$, at or below the lower end of several coherent-emission predictions for neutron-star mergers.
